items.body: We speak to the EU's Commissioner for Defence and Space, Andrius Kubilius. The former prime minister of Lithuania – who grew up during the Soviet era – tells us how he sees the confrontation between Europe and Russia. He also sounds the alarm over proposed cuts in the EU's future budget, saying that they could jeopardise major European projects in defence and space. Kubilius praises the EU's SAFE defence loans programme, remarking that it has been "really very successful".

items.title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
items.summary: The law faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

ByNadine Yousif

Senior Canada reporter

Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.

The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their funadamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.

The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely-watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

On Friday, the Supreme Court ruled that Quebec's use of the "notwithstanding clause" is valid, except for a section of Bill 21 that bars elected officials from wearing a face covering.

The court found that this provision of the law violates a section of the Canadian Charter protecting the democratic rights of all citizens, which is not covered by the notwithstanding clause.

Barring elected officials in Quebec's legislature from wearing a face covering would infringe on an individual's right to run for public office, the court found.

The court's majority also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the rights Charter even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.

translation.body:
图片来源，Getty Images

作者：Nadine Yousif

加拿大资深记者

加拿大最高法院基本维持了魁北克省一项禁止公共部门工作人员佩戴宗教标志（包括头巾和十字架）的法律。

这项名为第21号法案的法律面临来自多个群体的法律挑战，其中包括穆斯林、锡克教和天主教女教师，她们认为该法律侵犯了她们的基本权利。

魁北克省于2019年依据加拿大宪法中一项名为“但书条款”的独特机制通过了该法律——这是一个法律漏洞，允许政府凌驾于某些权利之上，例如宗教自由。

最高法院的这一裁决是加拿大历史上最受关注的裁决之一，其影响将在魁北克省和全国范围内都能感受到。

周五，最高法院裁定魁北克省使用“但书条款”有效，但第21号法案中禁止民选官员佩戴面部遮挡物的一项条款除外。

法院认定，该法律条款违反了《加拿大权利与自由宪章》中保护所有公民民主权利的部分，而该部分不受但书条款的约束。

法院认定，禁止魁北克省立法机构的民选官员佩戴面部遮挡物将侵犯个人竞选公职的权利。

法院多数意见还裁定，即使援引了但书条款，加拿大法院仍有权宣布一项法律是否符合《权利宪章》，但在本案中他们不会这样做。

items.title: Divisions deepen between EU member states after tense budget summit
items.summary: An EU leaders summit on the bloc's seven-year budget fell apart amid divisions over how to fund Ukraine. The budget proposal also includes a 3% tax on US tech companies, in a bid for the EU to generate additional funds.

EU leaders arrived in Brussels braced for a difficult showdown over the bloc's multitrillion-euro seven-year budget. But few expected the summit to unravel so quickly, with talks breaking down late on Thursday night.

Squabbles and thinly veiled public barbs meant they left without a deal and didn't even attempt to resume discussions on the planned second day.

There is a self-imposed deadline to find agreement before the end of 2026 on the budget which covers the 2028-2034 period. But experts say there is no cause for alarm, yet.

"Every time there are long-term EU budget negotiations, there are breakdowns, chaos, recrimination and a lot of political theater and drama," said Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, an EU economist and expert at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels.

The center of that political theater this time was the prime ministers of Denmark, Sweden, Belgium and Austria — countries wanting a reduced budget — who staged a walkout during smaller, group meetings, claiming the atmosphere had not been constructive to getting a deal.

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar called the whole summit "completely unnecessary," pointing the blame at the man who had decided to call it and whose job it is to meditate the talks, European Council President Antonio Costa.

Costa was diplomatic in defending his decision to bring the leaders to Brussels, telling the press: "For me it was very useful to figure out the parameters of a possible landing zone in December."

European Council President Antonio Costa was forced to defend his decision to call the summit which ended in acrimonyImage: Daniel Gnap/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Germany demands more for competitiveness, security, defense

Long before the summit started, Germany had laid down an ultimatum — Berlin would only sign off on the budget if all the other EU countries greenlit an additional €45 billion ($49 billion) support loan for Ukraine to fund the country in its war efforts through 2027.

Hungary, Czechia, Bulgaria and Slovakia have dug their heels in against the proposal, insisting that giving Ukraine money to buy weapons will prolong the war. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico even accused Germany of "blackmail."

Can Europe defend itself without the US?

As Europe's biggest economy, Germany's contribution amounts to around 25% of the whole budget.

In a press conference after the summit, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said "hundreds of billions" still need to be slashed. The European Commission's original proposal of approximately €1.786 trillion had already been reduced by €204 billion (down 10.2%).

"Europe needs to exercise a sense of proportion," said Merz. "The budget cannot grow indefinitely, and the burden of financing it must be distributed fairly."

Merz also aimed a comment toward Costa, who has been renewing the details in the budget proposal at every stage.

"The proposals that have been on the table so far are not a basis for an agreement," said Merz.

Costa did tell leaders on Thursday that he is planning to cut between €220 billion to €230 billion out of the next proposal.

Berlin's budget reduction push is backed by six other countries who together call themselves the "Sensible Seven." All pay more into the collective EU financial pot than they receive out of it.

The leaders of the 'sensible seven' — Germany, Netherlands, Denmark, Belgium, Sweden, Finland and Austria — met separately at the Brussels summitImage: Frederic Sierakowski

They are opposed by 17 EU member states who insist the total budget should grow, led by France and Italy. These countries call themselves the "Friends of Cohesion" — a nod to the EU cohesion funds which are used to share wealth from the EU's richer regions and nations to its poorer ones.

In the current proposal, agriculture, fisheries and cohesion spending falls from 59.1% to 42.4%, while money for economic competitiveness, security, and defense rises from 17.7% to 27.7%. This rebalancing is a key German demand.

EU looking elsewhere to raise funds

The EU is also searching for a way to add money into the budget that doesn't come from national contributions. The current proposal includes a controversial EU-wide digital tax which could chart a course for a major battle with the US.

The idea, originally put forward by French President Emmanuel Macron, is for a 3% tax on revenues of online advertising, online marketplaces and on the monetization of user data. The money, to be paid directly into the EU's budget, is estimated to bring in €5 billion per year.

But the proposal is ringing alarm bells in Ireland where US tech giants like Google, Meta, Apple, Microsoft and LinkedIn are headquartered.

"A digital tax is sending out all the wrong messages," said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin, who could still veto the proposal.

Protecting the EU's top triple-A rating

There is a fear in some European capitals that without being able to generate its own funds, future EU loans could downgrade the European Commission's unblemished standing on international markets.

The EU has around €860 billion in outstanding debts it took out for its pandemic recovery funding and to support Ukraine. Its triple-A credit rating could be downgraded if Marine le Pen, the far-right front-runner in France's presidential election, wins in the spring and follows through on her promise to reduce French contributions to the EU budget.

If France's far-right challenger wins the spring 2027 election, it could change the whole shape of the EU budget negotiationsImage: Stephanie Lecocq/REUTERS

EU member states that favor a financing model through national contributions rather than through tax revenue "understand very well what will happen if the EU loses its triple-A rating," said Bruegel's Kirkegaard. "Interest rate costs will go up even more. Who has to pay for that? Net contributing countries, like Germany, the Nordics, the Dutch, which is why they are much more open to this than in the past."

Other European tax experts believe that prior examples of these digital taxes show the costs outweigh the benefits.

"We analyzed the states which have a digital services tax [DST], and we've seen that economic cost exceeds the revenue generated," said Cristina Enache, an economist at the Brussels-based nonprofit Tax Foundation Europe. "Spain has a DST and the expected revenue was twice or three times larger than what they actually are collecting."

Enache called the tax proposal "politically impossible."

EU leaders know that the clock on their end-of-2026 deadline is ticking, and will return to the same conference rooms in late December hoping for a more conducive atmosphere to strike a deal.

translation.summary: 欧盟领导人就欧盟七年预算举行的峰会因在如何资助乌克兰问题上存在分歧而破裂。该预算提案还包括对美国科技公司征收3%的税，以期欧盟能够增加收入。

在 Google 上选择 DW

2026年11月峰会结束后，德国总理弗里德里希·默茨在布鲁塞尔向媒体阐述其政府立场。图片来源：Marius Burgelman/AP Photo/picture alliance

广告

欧盟领导人抵达布鲁塞尔，准备就该集团数万亿欧元的七年预算展开一场艰难的摊牌。但很少有人预料到峰会会如此迅速地瓦解，谈判在周四深夜破裂。

争吵和几乎不加掩饰的公开讥讽意味着他们离开时未能达成协议，甚至没有尝试在计划的第二天恢复讨论。

各方为自己设定了在2026年底前就涵盖2028-2034年期间的预算达成一致的期限。但专家表示，目前还没有理由恐慌。

“每次进行欧盟长期预算谈判，都会出现破裂、混乱、相互指责以及大量政治作秀和戏剧性场面，”欧盟经济学家、布鲁塞尔布鲁盖尔智库专家雅各布·芬克·柯克高说。

这一次政治作秀的中心是丹麦、瑞典、比利时和奥地利的总理——这些国家希望削减预算——他们在较小规模的小组会议期间退场，声称气氛不利于达成协议。

匈牙利总理彼得·马扎尔称整个峰会“完全没有必要”，并将矛头指向决定召开峰会、且职责是调解谈判的欧洲理事会主席安东尼奥·科斯塔。

科斯塔在为自己的决定辩护时表现得很有外交手腕，他对媒体说：“对我来说，弄清12月可能达成协议的着陆区参数非常有用。”

欧洲理事会主席安东尼奥·科斯塔被迫为召开这场以激烈争吵收场的峰会的决定辩护。图片来源：Daniel Gnap/NurPhoto/picture alliance

德国要求更多资金用于竞争力、安全和国防

早在峰会开始之前，德国就已发出最后通牒——柏林只有在所有其他欧盟国家批准向乌克兰提供额外450亿欧元（490亿美元）支持贷款、以资助该国到2027年的战争努力时，才会签署预算。

匈牙利、捷克、保加利亚和斯洛伐克坚决反对该提议，坚持认为给乌克兰钱购买武器会延长战争。斯洛伐克总理罗伯特·菲佐甚至指责德国“敲诈”。

欧洲能否在没有美国的情况下自卫？

作为欧洲最大经济体，德国的出资约占整个预算的25%。

在峰会后的新闻发布会上，德国总理弗里德里希·默茨表示，仍需削减“数千亿”。欧盟委员会最初约1.786万亿欧元的提案已被削减2040亿欧元（下降10.2%）。

“欧洲需要把握分寸，”默茨说。“预算不能无限增长，融资负担必须公平分配。”

默茨还将一句话指向科斯塔，后者在每个阶段都在更新预算提案的细节。

“迄今为止摆在桌上的提案不能作为达成协议的基础，”默茨说。

科斯塔周四确实告诉各国领导人，他计划从下一份提案中削减2200亿至2300亿欧元。

柏林削减预算的推动得到另外六个国家的支持，它们自称“理性七国”。这些国家向欧盟共同财政资金池缴纳的款项都多于它们从中获得的款项。

“理性七国”——德国、荷兰、丹麦、比利时、瑞典、芬兰和奥地利——的领导人已在布鲁塞尔峰会期间另行会晤。图片来源：Frederic Sierakowski

以法国和意大利为首的17个欧盟成员国反对它们，坚持预算总额应当增长。这些国家自称“凝聚力之友”——这是对欧盟凝聚力基金的呼应，该基金用于将财富从欧盟较富裕的地区和国家分享给较贫穷的地区和国家。

在当前提案中，农业、渔业和凝聚力支出从59.1%降至42.4%，而用于经济竞争力、安全和国防的资金从17.7%升至27.7%。这种再平衡是德国的关键要求。

欧盟另寻筹资途径

欧盟还在寻找不来自国家出资的预算增资方式。当前提案包括一项有争议的欧盟全境数字税，这可能为与美国的一场重大争斗铺路。

这一想法最初由法国总统埃马纽埃尔·马克龙提出，即对在线广告、在线市场以及用户数据变现的收入征收3%的税。这笔钱将直接缴入欧盟预算，估计每年带来50亿欧元收入。

但该提案在爱尔兰敲响了警钟，谷歌、Meta、苹果、微软和领英等美国科技巨头都在那里设有总部。

“数字税发出的全是错误信号，”爱尔兰总理米歇尔·马丁说，他仍可能否决该提案。

保护欧盟的最高AAA评级

一些欧洲国家首都担心，如果无法自行创收，未来的欧盟贷款可能会下调欧盟委员会在国际市场上完美无瑕的信用地位。

欧盟约有8600亿欧元未偿债务，这些债务是为其疫情复苏资金和支持乌克兰而借入的。如果法国总统选举中的极右翼领跑者玛丽娜·勒庞在春季获胜，并兑现其减少法国对欧盟预算出资的承诺，其AAA信用评级可能会被下调。

如果法国的极右翼挑战者在2027年春季选举中获胜，可能会改变欧盟预算谈判的整体格局。图片来源：Stephanie Lecocq/REUTERS

布鲁盖尔智库的柯克高表示，倾向于通过国家出资而非税收收入来融资的欧盟成员国“非常清楚如果欧盟失去AAA评级会发生什么”。“利率成本将进一步上升。谁来为此买单？净出资国，比如德国、北欧国家、荷兰，这就是为什么它们现在比过去更愿意接受这种做法。”

其他欧洲税收专家认为，这些数字税以往的实例表明成本大于收益。

“我们分析了征收数字服务税（DST）的国家，发现经济成本超过所产生的收入，”布鲁塞尔非营利组织欧洲税收基金会经济学家克里斯蒂娜·埃纳切说。“西班牙征收数字服务税，预期收入是实际征收额的两到三倍。”

埃纳切称该税收提案“在政治上不可能”。

欧盟领导人知道，2026年底最后期限的时钟正在滴答作响，他们将在12月下旬回到同样的会议室，希望届时气氛更有利于达成协议。

items.title: Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
items.summary: France's president made the comment while speaking to French farming representatives, months after the EU banned Brazil beef and poultry products.
items.body:
Image source, Tom Nicholson/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock

Image caption,

The French president said he was proud to have led efforts to ban Brazilian meat products

ByMallory Moench

Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron who called Brazilian meat "doped".

France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry which took effect in September.

In its statement, the Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".

Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat and poultry owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.

In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.

Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at Élysée Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.

"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.

Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".

Affirming its partnership with France was important, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".

Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.

Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at Élysée Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.

"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.
Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".

Affirming its partnership with France was important, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".
Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.

items.title: Dutch authorities seize 26 critically endangered turtles from luggage of passenger bound for Hong Kong
items.summary: The tiny Vallarta mud turtle was only discovered in 2018. It's critically endangered with around 300 thought to live in the wild. Almost one tenth of that number were stashed in a traveler's luggage, bound in duct tape.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5Pzto

Prefer DW on Google

Authorities in the Netherlands seized 26 of the critically endangered critters on November 21; that's equivalent to almost one-tenth of the entire population estimated to be at large in the wildImage: NVWA

Advertisement

The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said on Friday that it had seized more than two dozen critically endangered turtles that customs officers found in a passenger's luggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport.

The Vallarta mud turtles discovered in the luggage of a man flying to Hong Kong via Schiphol are endemic to Mexico. They were only formally discovered and catalogued in 2018 and are one of the smallest of all known genuses of turtle.

"These highly rare and protected turtles were presumably taken from the wild in Mexico, where an estimated population of only about 300 of these animals remain," the NVWA said in a press release.

How were the turtles discovered and smuggled?

Dutch customs agents discovered the animals on November 21 during a regular inspection and then alerted the NVWA, as the responsible agency for such cases, on realizing that they had uncovered live fauna.

Police then arrested the man at the NVWA's request, and the NVWA said in Friday's statement that he was still in custody, with federal prosecutors continuing their investigations.

"Most of the turtles were packed in a box alongside a toy car, while others were placed inside a sealed sock within a suitcase," the NVWA wrote. "The animals had been wrapped in duct tape, which prevented them from moving. All of the turtles survived the journey."

Authorities said the turtles were being housed at a specialized rescue facility, "where the duct tape was carefully removed," and where they were "receiving the care they require."

What are Vallarta mud turtles?

Vallarta mud turtles are exceptionally small freshwater turtles that only entered the taxonomical record in 2018, endemic to a very small area in western Mexico.

Relatively little is known about the creature owing both to its recent discovery and the damage to its habitat caused by urbanization and a growing tourist trade in the Mexican state of Jalisco.

The Turtle Island organization in Graz, Austria — which recently started breeding the turtles in Austria as a "genetic reservoir for eventual rewilding" and is working to help preserve them in Mexico — considers it "the world's smallest turtle species," and estimates that "over 99%" of its natural habitat has been lost to urbanization.

Roads and traffic are a particular risk for the slow-moving creatures.

"Despite strict protections, their small size and striking appearance make them prime targets for illegal collectors," Turtle Island says when detailing other risks to the tiny animals, that are not known to grow larger than 10 centimeters (less than 4 inches) in length.

The IUCN Red List classifies it as "Critically Endangered" and it is subject to the highest level of protection under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).

"The suspected poaching of 26 of these turtles from the wild may have reduced the population by nearly 10%," the NVWA wrote, basing its figure on the estimated population of around 300 of the turtles in the wild.

The agency urged people to report any suspected instances of illegal trade of protected animal or plant species, whether "via online forums, marketplaces, bird fairs, or antique and curiosity markets."

translation.summary: 微小的巴亚尔塔泥龟直到 2018 年才被发现。它极度濒危，据信野外仅存约 300 只。其中近十分之一的数量被藏在一名旅客的行李中，用胶带捆扎。
translation.label: 机器翻译
translation.summary_source: The tiny Vallarta mud turtle was only discovered in 2018. It's critically endangered with around 300 thought to live in the wild. Almost one tenth of that number were stashed in a traveler's luggage, bound in duct tape.
translation.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5Pzto

在谷歌上首选德国之声

荷兰当局于11月21日查获了26只极度濒危的动物；这相当于估计野外现存全部种群数量的近十分之一。图片来源：NVWA

广告

荷兰食品和消费品安全局（NVWA）周五表示，该局查获了二十多只极度濒危的乌龟，这些乌龟是海关人员在阿姆斯特丹史基浦机场一名乘客的行李中发现的。

这些在一名经史基浦飞往香港的男子的行李中发现的巴亚尔塔泥龟是墨西哥特有物种。它们直到2018年才被正式发现并记录在案，是所有已知龟属中体型最小的物种之一。

NVWA在一份新闻稿中表示：“这些极其稀有且受保护的乌龟推测是从墨西哥野外捕获的，那里估计仅存约300只这种动物。”

这些乌龟是如何被发现和走私的？

荷兰海关人员于11月21日的一次例行检查中发现了这些动物，并在意识到查获的是活体动物后，通知了负责此类案件的NVWA。

随后警方应NVWA的请求逮捕了该男子，NVWA在周五的声明中表示，他仍被拘留，联邦检察官正在继续调查。

NVWA写道：“大多数乌龟被装在一个盒子里，旁边放着一辆玩具车，其余的则被塞进手提箱内的一只密封袜子里。这些动物被胶带缠绕，无法动弹。所有乌龟都在这段旅程中存活了下来。”

当局表示，这些乌龟被安置在一个专门的救助设施中，“在那里胶带被小心地去除”，它们“正在接受所需的照料”。

什么是巴亚尔塔泥龟？

巴亚尔塔泥龟是一种体型极小的淡水龟，2018年才被纳入分类学记录，是墨西哥西部一个非常小区域的特有物种。

由于发现时间较近，加上墨西哥哈利斯科州城市化和日益增长的旅游业对其栖息地造成的破坏，人们对这种生物知之甚少。

奥地利格拉茨的龟岛组织最近开始在奥地利繁育这种乌龟，作为“最终野化放归的基因储备”，并致力于在墨西哥帮助保护它们。该组织认为它是“世界上最小的龟类”，并估计其“超过99%”的自然栖息地已因城市化而丧失。

道路和交通对这类行动缓慢的生物构成特别的风险。

龟岛组织在详述这种微小动物面临的其他风险时表示：“尽管受到严格保护，但它们体型小、外表醒目，使其成为非法采集者的主要目标。”据悉这种乌龟体长不超过10厘米（不到4英寸）。

世界自然保护联盟红色名录将其列为“极度濒危”，并根据《濒危野生动植物种国际贸易公约》（CITES）受到最高级别的保护。

NVWA写道：“涉嫌从野外盗猎26只这种乌龟，可能已使种群数量减少了近10%。”这一数字基于野外约300只乌龟的估计种群数量。

该机构敦促人们举报任何涉嫌非法交易受保护动植物物种的情况，无论是“通过网络论坛、市场、鸟类集市，还是古董和珍奇市场”。

items.title: Airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy, succumbing to aviation fuel costs
items.summary: The low-cost airline was only founded a few years ago and had been struggling to turn a profit. The spike in aviation fuel prices caused by the war in Iran has now driven Norway's Norse Atlantic into bankruptcy.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5Pzc8

Prefer DW on Google

Norse Atlantic Airways was a relative newcomer in the industry, founded in 2021 and airborne since 2022 [FILE: July 17, 2025]Image: dts-Agentur/picture alliance

Advertisement

Norwegian low-cost, long-haul airline Norse Atlantic's operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the carrier said on Friday.

The airline had warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical," and suspended all flights the following day, saying it was urgently seeking emergency funding to fend off bankruptcy.

Like many commercial airlines, Norse Atlantic is highly exposed to the vastly increased jet fuel prices of 2026, attributable in very large part to the war in Iran and resultant tension throughout the wider Middle East.

What did Norse Atlantic say about the bankruptcy filing?

Norse had said slightly earlier on Friday that its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier's fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back. Initially the company said it planned to contest this claim, which would have rendered it effectively unable to operate.

But the announcement of plans to file for bankruptcy followed fairly soon after.

"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution," Norse CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement.

Other companies in the group like the stock market-listed Norse Atlantic ASA parent company and the Norse Atlantic UK subsidiary are not part of the filing and are still attempting to stay in business, the company said.

"The board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald said.

The company said on Thursday that it planned to file for bankruptcy unless financing could be arranged and had warned: "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found."

Founded just five years ago and based in Arendal in Norway, Norse Atlantic had a fleet of 12 planes and serviced a total of 14 destinations. It had recorded a net loss of $61.9 million (€56.5 million) in 2025, even before the additional economic strains caused by the war in Iran.

Why has the war in Iran put such strain on the aviation industry?

Small and lower-cost airlines are struggling in particular, but the aviation industry in general is facing severe problems amid the strains on global fuel deliveries caused by the conflict in the Gulf.

In early 2026, as the US launched attacks on Iran — soon leading to reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — aviation fuel rapidly spiked, more than doubling in price at its peak.

It rose higher even than in the immediate aftermath of Russia's full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Although it dipped in mid-summer amid hopes of a resolution to the conflict, it rose once again as these faded and a stalemate developed.

This has posed the worst crisis for the industry since the COVID pandemic drastically reduced the volume of air traffic in 2020 and beyond, a much larger issue that many carriers were still struggling to recover from.

北欧大西洋航空是业内相对较新的公司，成立于2021年，自2022年开始运营 [资料图：2025年7月17日]图片来源：dts-Agentur/picture alliance

广告

挪威低成本长途航空公司北欧大西洋航空的运营实体已于周五宣布破产，该航空公司表示。

该航空公司曾在周三警告其财务状况“危急”，并于次日暂停所有航班，称正在紧急寻求应急资金以避免破产。

与许多商业航空公司一样，北欧大西洋航空高度暴露于2026年大幅上涨的航空燃油价格之下，这在很大程度上归因于伊朗战争以及由此引发的整个中东地区的紧张局势。

北欧大西洋航空对破产申请说了什么？

北欧大西洋航空在周五稍早时曾表示，其出租方已终止该航空公司全部12架飞机的租赁合同，并要求归还飞机。最初该公司表示计划对此提出异议，而此举实际上将使其无法运营。

但破产申请计划的宣布紧随其后。

“北欧大西洋航空AS的董事会尽管公司和集团为寻找解决方案做出了广泛努力，仍做出了申请破产的艰难决定，”北欧大西洋航空首席执行官埃温德·罗尔德在一份声明中表示。

该公司表示，集团旗下其他公司，如股票上市的北欧大西洋航空ASA母公司以及北欧大西洋航空英国子公司，不在破产申请范围内，仍在努力维持经营。

“上市实体北欧大西洋航空ASA及英国子公司的董事会、管理层和顾问正在努力为剩余业务寻找继续运营的解决方案，”罗尔德说。

该公司周四曾表示，除非能够安排融资，否则计划申请破产，并警告称：“无法保证会找到可行的解决方案。”

北欧大西洋航空成立仅五年，总部位于挪威阿伦达尔，拥有12架飞机，服务14个目的地。2025年，即便在伊朗战争造成额外经济压力之前，该公司已录得6190万美元（5650万欧元）的净亏损。

为什么伊朗战争给航空业带来如此大的压力？

小型和低成本航空公司尤其举步维艰，但受海湾冲突导致全球燃料供应紧张的影响，整个航空业都面临严重问题。

2026年初，随着美国对伊朗发动攻击——很快导致通过霍尔木兹海峡的交通减少——航空燃油价格迅速飙升，峰值时价格翻了一倍多。

其涨幅甚至高于2022年俄罗斯全面入侵乌克兰后的即时影响。尽管在夏季中期因对冲突解决的希望而有所回落，但随着希望消退和僵局形成，价格再次上涨。

这构成了该行业自2020年及以后新冠疫情大幅减少空中交通量以来最严重的危机，而许多航空公司仍在努力从这一更大的问题中恢复。

OSLO: Airline Norse Atlantic’s Norwegian operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the long-haul budget carrier said on Friday (Nov 27), succumbing to soaring fuel costs wrought by the war in Iran.

Norse Atlantic ASA, which is listed on the Oslo Euronext Expand bourse, and other group companies are not part of the filing and are still attempting to stay in business, the company said in a statement.

items.title: As Gambia gears up for election, can Barrow secure a third term?
items.summary: President Adama Barrow is seeking a third term as Gambians vote on December 5. The election will test the opposition's appeal and the country's progress on democratic reform.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PzVs

Prefer DW on Google

Barrow came ‌to power in 2017 after defeating longtime ruler Yahya JammehImage: ZOHRA BENSEMRA/REUTERS

Advertisement

Gambia votes on December 5 in a presidential election that takes place nearly 10 years after voters ended the 22-year rule of military ruler Yahya Jammeh.

President Adama Barrow, who succeeded Jammeh in 2017, is running for a third term despite an earlier pledge not to do so.

Barrow is running against the tiny West African country's main opposition leader Ousainou Darboe of the United Democratic Party, youth candidate Talib Ahmed Bensouda, who until last week was mayor of Kanifing Municipality, and five other candidates.

The field also includes independent candidates Almameh Gibba, a lawmaker who is backed by Jammeh, and former Vice President Isatou Touray, the only woman in the presidential race.

What matters to voters

Gambia is still governed under its 1997 constitution, which was adopted during Jammeh's rule.

A proposed replacement, which included presidential term limits, was rejected by the National Assembly in July 2025 after failing to secure the required three-quarter majority.

Barrow has defended his decision to seek a third term, saying voters should decide who leads the country. While he says he supports presidential term limits, he has argued that their introduction depends on securing enough parliamentary backing for a new constitution.

"I believe in term limits. And the Gambian people are the ones who elect a president," Barrow told reporters after submitting his nomination papers to the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) earlier in November. "So they decide the fate of a president and it is up to the Gambian people to decide whether I should be president for a third time or not."

Many Gambians have voiced concerns about a lack of economic opportunitiesImage: Zohra Bensemra/REUTERS

Opposition parties have said their focus is not only on defeating Barrow but also on ensuring the election is conducted fairly.

Lamin Manneh, the United Democratic Party's administrative secretary, said the party's immediate priority is to ensure that the IEC conducts credible elections.

"The IEC has the responsibility of putting Gambians into confidence, ensuring that they guarantee us a credible election, a free election and a fair election," said Manneh.

Political analyst Malang Faye said the campaign was still taking shape after the official period began on November 16.

"The incumbent is already ahead," he told DW. "Some of the parties are yet to start their campaign." But he cautioned against judging electoral support by rally attendance alone.

"A large crowd at a political rally does not necessarily mean the same level of support at the ballot box," Faye added, noting that the election will test whether the democratic transition that began in 2016 can be consolidated.

Jobs, cost of living top of mind

Many voters say their immediate concerns are jobs, affordable living costs and better public services.

What happens when you speak up?

The World Bank has projected economic growth of 5.3% in 2026, but said extreme poverty is expected to remain at about 21%.

The 2025 Labour Force Survey puts youth unemployment at 11.5%, while 41.3% of young people are not in employment, education or training.

The figures reflect concerns voiced by many young Gambians about the lack of economic opportunities.

Voter Alhagie Sama said young people need opportunities at home, rather than having to risk dangerous journeys abroad.

"We need a country where young people do not have to risk their lives crossing the Mediterranean Sea in search of opportunities," he said, adding that he wants the next government to deliver decent jobs, make basic necessities more affordable and improve access to health care and education.

Another voter and activist, Binta Bojang, said unemployment remains one of the country's biggest challenges.

"I would want the next president to prioritize employment, like particularly youth employment," she told DW, noting that joblessness goes beyond conventional definitions.

"We need to understand unemployment beyond the conventional definition, I mean the dictionary definition. Because unemployment definitely manifests differently in the lives of ordinary Gambians."

Election under observation

The Independent Electoral Commission has said 1,146,474 people are registered to vote. They will cast their ballots across 53 constituencies, 730 polling centers and 1,773 polling stations.

The commission has been training election officials in voting procedures, counting, verification and the transmission of results. It said the preparations are aimed at ensuring a peaceful and credible election.

International observers are also monitoring the process.

Following an invitation from Gambian authorities, the European Union has deployed an election observation mission, with teams of analysts and long-term observers across the country.

Gambia Election 2026: Can the opposition win?

The United Nations has also urged candidates to honor the peace pact signed on November 16.

"History will judge not what you sign today, but what you do tomorrow and in the days to come," Barrie Freeman, the UN's deputy special representative for West Africa and the Sahel, told candidates.

Under the pact, presidential candidates pledged "to respect the independence and constitutional mandate of the IEC, to cooperate with it throughout the electoral process, and to seek redress through lawful and appropriate channels should disputes arise."

The December 5 election will test not only Barrow's bid for another term, but also whether the democratic gains made since 2016 can be translated into lasting reforms and improved living conditions.

translation.title: 冈比亚筹备选举之际，巴罗能否赢得第三个任期？
translation.summary: 总统阿达马·巴罗正在寻求第三个任期，冈比亚人将于 12 月 5 日投票。此次选举将检验反对派的号召力以及该国在民主改革方面的进展。
translation.label: 机器翻译
translation.summary_source: President Adama Barrow is seeking a third term as Gambians vote on December 5. The election will test the opposition's appeal and the country's progress on democratic reform.
translation.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PzVs

在 Google 上首选 DW

巴罗在2017年击败长期统治者叶海亚·贾梅后上台执政。图片来源：ZOHRA BENSEMRA/路透社

广告

冈比亚将于12月5日举行总统选举，此时距离选民终结军事统治者叶海亚·贾梅长达22年的统治已近10年。

总统阿达马·巴罗于2017年接替贾梅，尽管此前曾承诺不再寻求连任，他此次仍竞选第三个任期。

巴罗的对手包括这个西非小国的主要反对党领袖、联合民主党的乌赛努·达尔博，青年候选人、直到上周还担任卡尼芬市市长的塔利布·艾哈迈德·本苏达，以及其他五名候选人。

参选者中还包括独立候选人、获贾梅支持的议员阿尔马梅·吉巴，以及前副总统伊萨图·图雷——她是总统竞选中唯一的女性。

选民关心什么

冈比亚仍依据其1997年宪法治理，该宪法是在贾梅统治期间通过的。

一项包含总统任期限制的拟议替代宪法，在未能获得所需四分之三多数支持后，于2025年7月被国民议会否决。

巴罗为其寻求第三个任期的决定进行了辩护，称应由选民决定谁来领导国家。他表示自己支持总统任期限制，但辩称是否引入任期限制取决于能否为新宪法争取到足够的议会支持。

“我相信任期限制。而冈比亚人民才是选举总统的人，”巴罗在11月早些时候向独立选举委员会（IEC）提交提名文件后对记者说。“所以由他们决定一位总统的命运，我是否应该第三次担任总统，要由冈比亚人民来决定。”

许多冈比亚人对缺乏经济机会表示担忧。图片来源：Zohra Bensemra/路透社

反对党表示，他们的重点不仅是击败巴罗，还在于确保选举公平进行。

联合民主党行政秘书拉明·曼内表示，该党的当务之急是确保独立选举委员会举行可信的选举。

“独立选举委员会有责任让冈比亚人建立信心，确保他们向我们保证一场可信、自由和公平的选举，”曼内说。

政治分析人士马朗·法耶表示，在11月16日正式竞选期开始后，竞选活动仍在成形之中。

“现任总统已经领先，”他对DW说。“一些政党尚未开始竞选。”但他告诫不要仅凭集会出席人数来判断选举支持率。

“政治集会上的一大群人并不一定意味着投票箱前也有同等程度的支持，”法耶补充说，并指出这次选举将检验2016年开始的民主转型能否得到巩固。

就业和生活成本最受关注

许多选民表示，他们最直接的关切是就业、可负担的生活成本和更好的公共服务。

发声之后会发生什么？

世界银行预测2026年经济增长率为5.3%，但表示极端贫困率预计仍将维持在约21%。

2025年劳动力调查显示，青年失业率为11.5%，而41.3%的年轻人未处于就业、教育或培训状态。

这些数字反映了许多冈比亚年轻人对缺乏经济机会的担忧。

选民阿尔哈吉·萨马表示，年轻人需要在本国的机会，而不必冒险踏上危险的出国之路。

“我们需要一个年轻人不必冒着生命危险穿越地中海寻找机会的国家，”他说，并补充说他希望下一届政府提供体面的工作、让基本生活必需品更可负担，并改善医疗和教育服务。

另一位选民兼活动人士宾塔·博江表示，失业仍是该国最大的挑战之一。

“我希望下一任总统优先考虑就业，尤其是青年就业，”她对DW说，并指出失业问题超出了常规定义。

“我们需要在常规定义——我是说字典定义——之外理解失业。因为失业在普通冈比亚人的生活中显然有着不同的表现。”

选举受到观察

独立选举委员会表示，共有1,146,474人登记投票。他们将在53个选区、730个投票中心和1,773个投票站投票。

该委员会一直在培训选举官员，内容涉及投票程序、计票、核验和结果传输。委员会表示，这些准备工作旨在确保选举和平、可信。

国际观察员也在监督这一进程。

应冈比亚当局邀请，欧盟已部署选举观察团，分析人员和长期观察员团队分布在全国各地。

冈比亚2026年选举：反对党能赢吗？

联合国也敦促候选人遵守11月16日签署的和平公约。

“历史评判的不是你们今天签署了什么，而是你们明天以及未来几天会做什么，”联合国负责西非和萨赫勒地区事务的副特别代表巴里·弗里曼对候选人说。

根据该公约，总统候选人承诺“尊重独立选举委员会的独立性和宪法授权，在整个选举过程中与其合作，并在出现争议时通过合法适当的渠道寻求补救”。

12月5日的选举不仅将检验巴罗争取连任的努力，也将检验2016年以来取得的民主成果能否转化为持久改革和生活条件的改善。

items.title: Informer TV owner Vucicevic arrested: Has the reckoning with Serbia's pro-Vucic media machine begun?
items.summary: The arrest of media owner Dragan J. Vucicevic raises questions about whether Serbia is holding the people behind the country's pro-Vucic media accountable — or whether this is another political power struggle.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5Pz4c

Prefer DW on Google

Dragan J. Vucicevic, owner and editor-in-chief of Informer TV, was arrested on November 25 and remanded in custody for 30 days. He is pictured here earlier this monthImage: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

Advertisement

"Beat them! Break their ribs," shouted the man in the studio during a live TV broadcast.

The man in question was Dragan J. Vucicevic, editor-in-chief of the channel Informer TV, and he was urging police officers to use force against demonstrators during a major student protest in June 2025.

On November 25, Vucicevic was arrested by police on suspicion of causing panic and disorder and obstructing justice. According to the authorities, his appearances "created an atmosphere of public lynching," and he labeled 97 citizens as enemies of the state.

The authorities cite instances where he described protesters as "scum," "hyenas" and "vultures," and spread claims that the students were preparing a "bloodbath" and a "civil war."

Ready to break free: How Serbia's media are changing

The prosecution says that between 2023 and 2026, Vucicevic systematically used Informer TV to conduct a campaign that incited hatred and targeted activists, independent journalists and political opponents of the previous government.

Who is Dragan J. Vucicevic?

Vucicevic's arrest comes at a time of profound political change in Serbia.

Following the Student List's victory in the parliamentary election in late October and the end of the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) 14-year rule, questions have arisen about the accountability of people who were part of the previous political and institutional system.

Critics have described Vucicevic as the mouthpiece of former President Aleksandar Vucic — a man who said publicly what the president was thinking but could not say himself because of the office he held.

"He [Vucicevic] is someone who stopped being a journalist a long time ago, and I think he crossed the line of being merely a propagandist some time ago. He was, in fact, a weapon in the hands of Aleksandar Vucic and his party," said Ivana Stevanovic of the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, a Belgrade-based organization that provides media support and fights for press freedom. It is named after a Serbian journalist who was killed in 1999.

Stevanovic told DW that Vucicevic used his media platforms to "target and endanger people, spread falsehoods that threatened their safety," all as part of a campaign against political opponents, journalists and media outlets who were critical of the government's record.

Protesters in April 2025 called for media freedom and adherence to ethical standards outside the offices of the tabloid newspaper Informer. The sign on the left reads 'Colorful (fake) revolution? Colorful lie.' The sign on the right: 'Bottom, bottom of the bottom, des-Informer' Image: SPASA DAKIC/SIPA/picture alliance

"This man showed a female student's intimate photographs live on air. He stalked people. He had his notorious 'Viewer Intelligence Service,' which secretly followed people and filmed them in their everyday lives, then turned that material into disgusting reports," she said.

"We had calls for violence, threats and insults against prosecutors who were doing their jobs and judges who were issuing lawful rulings, expressed in indescribable language. We had wiretapping, recordings of conversations in restaurants presented as conspiracies to overthrow the state. Media outlets and journalists were accused of plotting to assassinate the president, while their reporting was portrayed as treason and selling out Kosovo," she told DW, adding that "the entire television channel is one big criminal offense."

Court cases and compensation

The Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) has already issued several warnings and temporarily halted the broadcasting of certain programs on Informer TV.

Journalists' and media associations, civil society organizations and representatives of academia have launched an initiative to have the channel's broadcasting license revoked.

According to the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, more than 1,000 court cases concerning the protection of reputation and honor have been brought against Informer in recent years.

"Of the cases concluded over the past three years, courts upheld the claims in 92% of them," said Stevanovic. "Compensation was awarded to people whose rights had been violated. Informer even paid damages to the same individuals several times for the same lies, which it kept publishing about them. None of these financial penalties made them stop."

Members of the Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) met on November 4 to discuss an initiative to revoke TV Informer's broadcasting licenseImage: Milan Ilic/SIPA/picture alliance

On one occasion, Dragan J. Vucicevic himself asked REM to impose a financial penalty on him rather than ban part of his program.

Money, it seems, was not a problem for Insajder Tim, the company behind all Informer media platforms (a daily tabloid newspaper, a television channel and an online portal).

Where did the money come from?

According to an investigation by Raskrikavanje, a fact-checking website that monitors the output of Serbian media, Insajder Tim, received around €273,000 ($299,000) in public funds in 2024 alone through public procurement contracts, advertising and media project funding.

Representatives of the Student List have claimed that the state-owned telecommunications company Telekom Srbija paid Informer between €500,000 and €700,000 a month.

Telekom Srbija, which also owns a cable network distributing television channels to millions of users in Serbia, cited business confidentiality when asked about the details of its cooperation with Informer.

SNS lawmakers protest

Vucicevic and his lawyers reject the accusations.

The defense argues that the proceedings amount to punishing someone for words they have spoken and raise questions about the boundary between freedom of expression and criminal liability.

Former President Aleksandar Vucic said Vucicevic had been arrested solely because of his journalistic work. SNS lawmakers walked out of a parliamentary session following news of the arrest and gathered outside the police station where the Informer editor was being held.

On the day after the October 25 parliamentary election, protestors confronted Dragan J. Vucicevic (center) in the offices of InformerImage: @veljars/TikTok/REUTERS

Stevanovic maintains that by arresting Vucicevic, Serbia is fulfilling its international obligations, including those arising from the European Convention on Human Rights and international conventions protecting civil and political rights.

"What constitutes a call for violence and a threat to democracy, security and health must be sanctioned and removed from the public sphere," she said.

A reckoning or an internal power struggle?

Vucicevic has been remanded in custody for 30 days.

The offence of causing panic and disorder through the media carries a prison sentence of between six months and five years.

Stevanovic points out, however, that the outcome of the case is not certain because the executive branch, the police and the Ministry of the Interior formally remain under the control of the outgoing government until such time as the Student List forms a new cabinet.

"What is happening now could be an internal power struggle within their own ranks, or an attempt by some prosecutors to clean up their records and ingratiate themselves with the new authorities, assuming what their wishes and intentions regarding Informer might be," she said. "Or it could be a serious manipulation, a staged arrest designed to portray Serbia abroad as a country carrying out revolutionary terror, which, of course, is not true."

"Beat them! Break their ribs," shouted the man in the studio during a live TV broadcast.

The man in question was Dragan J. Vucicevic, editor-in-chief of the channel Informer TV, and he was urging police officers to use force against demonstrators during a major student protest in June 2025.

On November 25, Vucicevic was arrested by police on suspicion of causing panic and disorder and obstructing justice. According to the authorities, his appearances "created an atmosphere of public lynching," and he labeled 97 citizens as enemies of the state.
The authorities cite instances where he described protesters as "scum," "hyenas" and "vultures," and spread claims that the students were preparing a "bloodbath" and a "civil war."
Ready to break free: How Serbia's media are changing

The prosecution says that between 2023 and 2026, Vucicevic systematically used Informer TV to conduct a campaign that incited hatred and targeted activists, independent journalists and political opponents of the previous government.
Who is Dragan J. Vucicevic?
Vucicevic's arrest comes at a time of profound political change in Serbia.

Following the Student List's victory in the parliamentary election in late October and the end of the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) 14-year rule, questions have arisen about the accountability of people who were part of the previous political and institutional system.

Critics have described Vucicevic as the mouthpiece of former President Aleksandar Vucic — a man who said publicly what the president was thinking but could not say himself because of the office he held.

"He [Vucicevic] is someone who stopped being a journalist a long time ago, and I think he crossed the line of being merely a propagandist some time ago. He was, in fact, a weapon in the hands of Aleksandar Vucic and his party," said Ivana Stevanovic of the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, a Belgrade-based organization that provides media support and fights for press freedom. It is named after a Serbian journalist who was killed in 1999.

Stevanovic told DW that Vucicevic used his media platforms to "target and endanger people, spread falsehoods that threatened their safety," all as part of a campaign against political opponents, journalists and media outlets who were critical of the government's record.

Protesters in April 2025 called for media freedom and adherence to ethical standards outside the offices of the tabloid newspaper Informer. The sign on the left reads 'Colorful (fake) revolution? Colorful lie.' The sign on the right: 'Bottom, bottom of the bottom, des-Informer' Image: SPASA DAKIC/SIPA/picture alliance

"This man showed a female student's intimate photographs live on air. He stalked people. He had his notorious 'Viewer Intelligence Service,' which secretly followed people and filmed them in their everyday lives, then turned that material into disgusting reports," she said.

"We had calls for violence, threats and insults against prosecutors who were doing their jobs and judges who were issuing lawful rulings, expressed in indescribable language. We had wiretapping, recordings of conversations in restaurants presented as conspiracies to overthrow the state. Media outlets and journalists were accused of plotting to assassinate the president, while their reporting was portrayed as treason and selling out Kosovo," she told DW, adding that "the entire television channel is one big criminal offense."
Court cases and compensation
The Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) has already issued several warnings and temporarily halted the broadcasting of certain programs on Informer TV.
Journalists' and media associations, civil society organizations and representatives of academia have launched an initiative to have the channel's broadcasting license revoked.
According to the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, more than 1,000 court cases concerning the protection of reputation and honor have been brought against Informer in recent years.

"Of the cases concluded over the past three years, courts upheld the claims in 92% of them," said Stevanovic. "Compensation was awarded to people whose rights had been violated. Informer even paid damages to the same individuals several times for the same lies, which it kept publishing about them. None of these financial penalties made them stop."
Members of the Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) met on November 4 to discuss an initiative to revoke TV Informer's broadcasting licenseImage: Milan Ilic/SIPA/picture alliance
On one occasion, Dragan J. Vucicevic himself asked REM to impose a financial penalty on him rather than ban part of his program.
Money, it seems, was not a problem for Insajder Tim, the company behind all Informer media platforms (a daily tabloid newspaper, a television channel and an online portal).
Where did the money come from?

According to an investigation by Raskrikavanje, a fact-checking website that monitors the output of Serbian media, Insajder Tim, received around €273,000 ($299,000) in public funds in 2024 alone through public procurement contracts, advertising and media project funding.
Representatives of the Student List have claimed that the state-owned telecommunications company Telekom Srbija paid Informer between €500,000 and €700,000 a month.

Telekom Srbija, which also owns a cable network distributing television channels to millions of users in Serbia, cited business confidentiality when asked about the details of its cooperation with Informer.
SNS lawmakers protest
Vucicevic and his lawyers reject the accusations.
The defense argues that the proceedings amount to punishing someone for words they have spoken and raise questions about the boundary between freedom of expression and criminal liability.

Former President Aleksandar Vucic said Vucicevic had been arrested solely because of his journalistic work. SNS lawmakers walked out of a parliamentary session following news of the arrest and gathered outside the police station where the Informer editor was being held.
On the day after the October 25 parliamentary election, protestors confronted Dragan J. Vucicevic (center) in the offices of InformerImage: @veljars/TikTok/REUTERS

Stevanovic maintains that by arresting Vucicevic, Serbia is fulfilling its international obligations, including those arising from the European Convention on Human Rights and international conventions protecting civil and political rights.
"What constitutes a call for violence and a threat to democracy, security and health must be sanctioned and removed from the public sphere," she said.
A reckoning or an internal power struggle?
Vucicevic has been remanded in custody for 30 days.
The offence of causing panic and disorder through the media carries a prison sentence of between six months and five years.

Stevanovic points out, however, that the outcome of the case is not certain because the executive branch, the police and the Ministry of the Interior formally remain under the control of the outgoing government until such time as the Student List forms a new cabinet.

"What is happening now could be an internal power struggle within their own ranks, or an attempt by some prosecutors to clean up their records and ingratiate themselves with the new authorities, assuming what their wishes and intentions regarding Informer might be," she said. "Or it could be a serious manipulation, a staged arrest designed to portray Serbia abroad as a country carrying out revolutionary terror, which, of course, is not true."

https://p.dw.com/p/5Pz4c

在谷歌上优先选择德国之声

Informer电视台的老板兼总编辑德拉甘·J·武契切维奇于11月25日被捕，并被还押候审30天。图为本月早些时候的他。图片来源：Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

广告

"打他们！打断他们的肋骨，"那名男子在一次电视直播中在演播室里喊道。

此人正是Informer电视台的总编辑德拉甘·J·武契切维奇，他当时正在敦促警察在2025年6月一场大规模学生抗议活动中对示威者使用武力。

11月25日，武契切维奇因涉嫌制造恐慌和混乱以及妨碍司法而被警方逮捕。据当局称，他的出镜"营造了一种公开私刑的氛围"，并将97名公民列为国家公敌。

当局列举了他将抗议者描述为"人渣"、"鬣狗"和"秃鹫"，并散布学生正在准备"血洗"和"内战"说法的实例。

准备挣脱束缚：塞尔维亚的媒体正在如何改变

检方称，在2023年至2026年间，武契切维奇系统性地利用Informer电视台开展了一场煽动仇恨的运动，针对活动人士、独立记者和前政府的政治对手。

德拉甘·J·武契切维奇是谁？

武契切维奇被捕之际，塞尔维亚正经历深刻的政治变革。

在10月下旬学生名单党赢得议会选举、塞尔维亚进步党（SNS）14年统治结束后，人们开始质疑曾属于前政治和制度体系的人士的问责问题。

批评者将武契切维奇描述为前总统亚历山大·武契奇的喉舌——一个公开说出总统心中所想、但总统因职位所限无法亲口说出的人。

"他（武契切维奇）早就不是一个记者了，我认为他很久以前就越过了仅仅作为宣传者的界限。事实上，他是亚历山大·武契奇及其政党手中的一件武器，"斯拉夫科·丘鲁维亚基金会的伊万娜·斯特万诺维奇说。该基金会总部位于贝尔格莱德，提供媒体支持并为新闻自由而奋斗，以1999年遇害的一名塞尔维亚记者命名。

斯特万诺维奇告诉德国之声，武契切维奇利用其媒体平台"针对并危及他人，散布威胁他们安全的谎言"，这一切都是针对政治对手、记者和批评政府记录的媒体机构运动的一部分。

2025年4月，抗议者在小报《Informer》办公室外呼吁新闻自由和遵守道德标准。左侧标语写着"多彩的（假）革命？多彩的谎言。"右侧标语："底层，底层的底层，去-Informer" 图片来源：SPASA DAKIC/SIPA/picture alliance

"这个人曾在直播中展示一名女学生的私密照片。他跟踪他人。他有臭名昭著的'观众情报局'，秘密跟踪他人并拍摄他们的日常生活，然后将这些素材制作成令人作呕的报道，"她说。

"我们曾有过针对正在履行职责的检察官和正在作出合法裁决的法官的暴力呼吁、威胁和侮辱，用难以形容的语言表达。我们有过窃听、在餐厅的对话录音被呈现为推翻国家的阴谋。媒体机构和记者被指控密谋暗杀总统，而他们的报道被描绘成叛国和出卖科索沃，"她告诉德国之声，并补充说"整个电视台就是一个巨大的犯罪行为。"

法庭案件与赔偿

电子媒体监管局（REM）已多次发出警告，并暂时停止了Informer电视台某些节目的播出。

记者和媒体协会、民间社会组织以及学术界代表发起了一项倡议，要求吊销该频道的播出许可证。

据斯拉夫科·丘鲁维亚基金会称，近年来针对Informer提起了1000多起涉及保护名誉和荣誉的法庭案件。

"在过去三年已审结的案件中，法院在92%的案件中支持了诉讼请求，"斯特万诺维奇说。"权利受到侵犯的人获得了赔偿。Informer甚至多次因持续刊登关于同一批人的相同谎言而向他们支付损害赔偿金。这些经济处罚都没有让他们停止。"

电子媒体监管局（REM）成员于11月4日开会讨论吊销Informer电视台播出许可证的倡议 图片来源：Milan Ilic/SIPA/picture alliance

有一次，德拉甘·J·武契切维奇本人要求REM对他处以罚款，而不是禁播他的部分节目。

对于拥有所有Informer媒体平台（一份日报小报、一个电视频道和一个在线门户网站）的公司Insajder Tim来说，金钱似乎不是问题。

钱从哪里来？

据监测塞尔维亚媒体产出的事实核查网站Raskrikavanje的调查，仅2024年，Insajder Tim就通过公共采购合同、广告和媒体项目资助获得了约27.3万欧元（29.9万美元）的公共资金。

学生名单党的代表声称，国有电信公司塞尔维亚电信每月向Informer支付50万至70万欧元。

塞尔维亚电信还拥有一个向塞尔维亚数百万用户分发电视频道的有线网络，在被问及其与Informer合作的细节时，以商业机密为由拒绝透露。

SNS议员抗议

武契切维奇及其律师否认这些指控。

辩方认为，这些诉讼相当于因某人说过的话而惩罚他，并引发了关于言论自由与刑事责任之间界限的疑问。

前总统亚历山大·武契奇表示，武契切维奇被捕仅仅是因为他的新闻工作。SNS议员在得知逮捕消息后退出议会会议，并聚集在关押这位Informer编辑的警察局外。

10月25日议会选举后的第二天，抗议者在Informer办公室与德拉甘·J·武契切维奇（中）对峙 图片来源：@veljars/TikTok/REUTERS

斯特万诺维奇坚持认为，通过逮捕武契切维奇，塞尔维亚正在履行其国际义务，包括《欧洲人权公约》和保护公民及政治权利的国际公约所产生的义务。

"构成暴力呼吁以及对民主、安全和健康的威胁的行为必须受到制裁并从公共领域清除，"她说。

清算还是内部权力斗争？

武契切维奇已被还押候审30天。

通过媒体制造恐慌和混乱的罪行可判处六个月至五年监禁。

然而，斯特万诺维奇指出，案件结果并不确定，因为在学生名单党组建新内阁之前，行政部门、警察和内政部在形式上仍处于即将离任的政府控制之下。

"现在发生的事情可能是他们自己阵营内部的权力斗争，也可能是一些检察官试图洗清自己的记录并讨好新当局，揣测新当局对Informer可能抱有的愿望和意图，"她说。"或者这可能是一场严重的操纵，一场精心策划的逮捕，旨在向国外将塞尔维亚描绘成一个正在实施革命恐怖的国家，而这当然不是真的。"

广告

items.title: Duterte's ICC trial: What is at stake for the Philippines?
items.summary: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could determine the political fortunes of a powerful dynasty. Victims' families hope to see justice.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PzKr

Duterte was elected president in 2016 following a populist campaign in which he promised to kill criminals and drug dealersImage: Piroschka van de Wouw/REUTERS/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Advertisement

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on November 30, where he faces three counts of crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on drugs.

For the families of the thousands killed during his anti-narcotics campaign, the trial is a chance for justice that has eluded them at home.

It is also a significant test of international justice at a time when the ICC faces increasing political pressure and questions about its ability to hold former heads of state accountable.

Yet, Duterte, 81, is still a popular figure in the Philippines, where many still regard his violent crackdown as one of his presidency's greatest achievements.

With his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, a frontrunner for the 2028 presidential election, the proceedings in The Hague could become a defining issue in the Philippines' next presidential election.

Why is Duterte on trial?

Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016 following an expletive-laden, populist campaign in which he openly promised to kill criminals and drug dealers.

During his more than two decades as mayor of Davao City, he earned a reputation for transforming a notoriously violent city into a relatively safe one.

Filipino woman who lost family to drug war takes on Duterte

However, human rights groups found systematic extrajudicial killings by the so-called Davao Death Squad, which ICC prosecutors allege Duterte helped establish and oversee.

His disregard for political convention and promises of swift, uncompromising justice appealed to millions of Filipinos frustrated by corruption, crime and the perceived failures of successive governments.

"Filipinos who were deeply frustrated with everyday experiences of injustice and government inaction made them receptive to Duterte's promise of swift justice, even though extraordinary and violent means," Cleve Arguelles, a political scientist and CEO of Momentum Research, a pollster, told DW.

After assuming the presidency, Duterte extended his Davao law enforcement model nationwide. Police launched sweeping anti-narcotics operations, primarily targeting impoverished urban communities, while suspected drug users and dealers were also killed by unidentified gunmen.

A 'way of governing'

Philippine authorities officially recorded 6,252 deaths during anti-drug operations, with police claiming to have acted in self-defence. Human rights organizations estimate the actual death toll at between 12,000 and 30,000.

"Duterte's ruthless war on drugs was not simply a campaign against crime; it was a way of governing through killing," David Johnson, a professor of sociology at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told DW.

"The extraordinary violence he ordered and encouraged was sustained by a combination of extraordinary problems of impunity in the Philippine criminal justice system and deep failures of democracy in that country,” Johnson said.

"These conditions made extrajudicial killing politically useful even though it was ineffective as crime control," he added.

Duterte also used state power to intimidate and suppress wide sections of Philippine society, including opposition politicians, civil society groups, journalists, lawyers and judges, Diane Desierto, a professor of law and global affairs at the University of Notre Dame, told DW.

Former president remains popular

The deterioration of human rights under Duterte damaged the Philippines' international standing and strained relations with its traditional Western partners, particularly the United States under President Barack Obama and the European Union, which threatened to withdraw Manila's preferential trade privilege.

Duterte left office in June 2022 as one of the most popular presidents in recent Philippine history. A survey conducted by pollster Social Weather Stations found that 88% of Filipinos were satisfied with his performance.

His daughter was overwhelmingly elected vice president in May 2022, while their allies dominated that year's Senate elections.

"Up to now, the Dutertes remain popular not in spite of the drug war but because of it,” Arguelles said.

Why was Duterte arrested?

Despite years of domestic and international scrutiny, Duterte remained at liberty for nearly three years after leaving office.

The ICC opened a preliminary examination into the drug war in 2018, prompting Duterte to withdraw the Philippines from the court's founding treaty. A formal investigation began in September 2021.

For much of his early presidency, President Ferdinand Marcos refused to cooperate with the ICC investigation.

What changed was the breakdown of relations between the Marcoses and the Dutertes, two of the country's most powerful political dynasties.

Marcos' father had ruled the Philippines as a dictator until he was overthrown in the 1986 People Power Revolution.

Philippine cafe keeps alive memory of 'drug war' victims

The alliance that brought Marcos Jr. and Sara Duterte to power in 2022 unravelled spectacularly after November 2024, when the vice president claimed she had arranged for Marcos to be assassinated in the event of her own killing. She has since faced successive impeachment efforts.

Philippine authorities arrested Rodrigo Duterte in March 2025, acting on an ICC arrest warrant issued four days earlier.

In April this year, ICC judges confirmed three charges of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder.

The trial will begin with opening statements, followed by testimony from prosecution witnesses. The process is expected to be extensive, potentially running until 2028, the year of the next Philippine presidential elections.

What does the trial mean for Philippine politics?

The Philippines is effectively confronting two different questions about the Duterte legacy: whether Rodrigo Duterte should be held criminally accountable for his presidency and whether his family should be entrusted with political power again, Arguelles said.

Duterte-aligned senators implicated in the ICC investigation could face arrest and transfer to The Hague, while Sara Duterte is still a leading contender for the 2028 presidency, despite an ongoing impeachment trial over allegations of unexplained wealth that could see her barred from public office.

Her brother, Sebastian Duterte, the mayor of Davao City, has also become a possible alternative presidential candidate.

DW speaks with Nobel laureate Maria Ressa

By portraying the ICC proceedings as foreign interference and political persecution, the Duterte family hopes to preserve the political capital accumulated during Rodrigo Duterte's presidency, Jayson Lamchek, a legal scholar at Western Sydney University, told DW.

Before her father's arrest, Sara Duterte's performance and trust ratings had been declining amid allegations that she had misused confidential government funds.

However, her ratings rebounded following his detention and have largely held up despite the ongoing impeachment controversies, Ronald Holmes, a political science professor at De La Salle University and president of polling firm Pulse Asia Research, told DW.

"A conviction or prolonged trial near election season will likely turn the 2028 vote into a direct referendum on the Duterte legacy, either rallying sympathetic voters against perceived foreign and domestic persecution or galvanizing opposition forces around demands for accountability," Holmes said.

For many Filipinos, however, the trial's significance goes well beyond the political rivalry between the two dynasties.

"Rodrigo Duterte's trial in the ICC is a milestone not only for the victims and families of the war on drugs but for the entire country," Jean Encinas-Franco, a professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told DW.

"Duterte and his cabal ruled by fear and misogyny and held Filipinos under his iron grip. The Filipino people deserve an answer. The Filipino people deserve justice," she added.

In April this year, ICC judges confirmed three charges of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder.

The trial will begin with opening statements, followed by testimony from prosecution witnesses. The process is expected to be extensive, potentially running until 2028, the year of the next Philippine presidential elections.
What does the trial mean for Philippine politics?

The Philippines is effectively confronting two different questions about the Duterte legacy: whether Rodrigo Duterte should be held criminally accountable for his presidency and whether his family should be entrusted with political power again, Arguelles said.

Duterte-aligned senators implicated in the ICC investigation could face arrest and transfer to The Hague, while Sara Duterte is still a leading contender for the 2028 presidency, despite an ongoing impeachment trial over allegations of unexplained wealth that could see her barred from public office.
Her brother, Sebastian Duterte, the mayor of Davao City, has also become a possible alternative presidential candidate.
DW speaks with Nobel laureate Maria Ressa

By portraying the ICC proceedings as foreign interference and political persecution, the Duterte family hopes to preserve the political capital accumulated during Rodrigo Duterte's presidency, Jayson Lamchek, a legal scholar at Western Sydney University, told DW.
Before her father's arrest, Sara Duterte's performance and trust ratings had been declining amid allegations that she had misused confidential government funds.

However, her ratings rebounded following his detention and have largely held up despite the ongoing impeachment controversies, Ronald Holmes, a political science professor at De La Salle University and president of polling firm Pulse Asia Research, told DW.

"A conviction or prolonged trial near election season will likely turn the 2028 vote into a direct referendum on the Duterte legacy, either rallying sympathetic voters against perceived foreign and domestic persecution or galvanizing opposition forces around demands for accountability," Holmes said.
For many Filipinos, however, the trial's significance goes well beyond the political rivalry between the two dynasties.

"Rodrigo Duterte's trial in the ICC is a milestone not only for the victims and families of the war on drugs but for the entire country," Jean Encinas-Franco, a professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told DW.
"Duterte and his cabal ruled by fear and misogyny and held Filipinos under his iron grip. The Filipino people deserve an answer. The Filipino people deserve justice," she added.

items.title: In Iran, child marriage risks complicated by war
items.summary: War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates have warned.
items.body:

Early marriage often disrupts girls' education and opportunities Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Advertisement

For a girl still at school, marriage can mean leaving her education behind, becoming pregnant before adulthood and growing dependent on her family and husband.

In Iran, rights advocates warn that war and mounting financial hardship could expose more girls to those risks.

The warning comes as the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage is observed on November 27. The day was established during the UN General Assembly in 2025.

Although there is no evidence linking child marriages to the war, cases illustrate the danger faced by girls married as children, often with limited means of escaping abuse. Gaps in Iran's marriage statistics also make it difficult to measure the impact of the conflict.

In one case cited by the Iranian human rights news agency HRANA, a 14-year-old girl in Kerman province who had recently given birth was reportedly killed by her husband. Skylar Thompson, deputy director of Human Rights Activists in Iran, said the girl had reportedly been forced to marry at 13.

"While these cases cannot be directly attributed to the war, there are substantial grounds for concern that deteriorating socioeconomic conditions are placing more girls at risk," Thompson told DW.

What the figures show

Iran Open Data's analysis of the Civil Registration Organization's statistical yearbook identified 14,039 registered marriages involving girls under 15 between roughly March 2025 and March 2026. They accounted for just over 3% of all registered marriages.

The figure excludes girls aged 15 to 17. UNICEF defines child marriage as a formal marriage or informal union involving someone under 18.

Thompson said 31,646 marriages involving girls under 15 were registered in 2020–2021, indicating a longer-term decline in recorded cases.

But the latest figures largely predate the war, which began on February 28, 2026.

"The absence of recent, disaggregated statistics, coupled with the prevalence of unregistered marriages, makes it difficult to determine whether child marriage has increased since the outbreak of the war," she said.

When marriage becomes an economic calculation

The conflict has intensified pressures that can contribute to child marriage: lost income, difficulty staying in school and girls' financial dependence on their families.

In its October assessment, the World Bank described damage to infrastructure, disrupted trade and declining purchasing power, forecasting a 7.7% economic contraction in 2026/27.

Thompson said that families facing severe hardship may see marriage as a way to reduce household expenses, transfer financial responsibility or secure their daughters' future. Government-backed marriage loans can also create financial incentives for some disadvantaged families to arrange marriages involving minors, she added.

Iran uprising seen through the eyes of Iranian women

Hossein Raeesi, a lawyer and adjunct professor in Carleton University's Department of Law and Legal Studies in Ottawa, Canada, described a similar risk.

When families cannot meet a girl's living costs and education or other prospects are unavailable, they may push her toward marriage or force her into it, he told DW, while acknowledging that statistics on changes in numbers of child marriages since the war are still unavailable.

War and displacement

Displacement can further weaken children's access to education and protection. On March 12, the UN refugee agency estimated that up to 3.2 million people had been temporarily displaced within Iran, based on preliminary assessments. That was an early-war estimate, rather than a current displacement figure.

Thompson said displacement and disrupted schooling could isolate girls from teachers, social workers and others who might recognize pressure to marry and intervene on their behalf.

Financial dependence, limited independent legal assistance and insufficient shelters can leave girls with few alternatives, particularly when those arranging a marriage are also their legal guardians.

Few legal safeguards against child marriage

Article 1041 of Iran's Civil Code allows girls under 13 and boys under 15 to marry with guardian consent and court approval. Iranian law therefore provides no blanket prohibition on marriage below the age of 18.

"Although Iranian law formally recognizes consent as a condition of marriage, it provides inadequate practical safeguards against familial coercion," Thompson told DW.

Raeesi said preventing a marriage was insufficient if a girl remained under pressure at home. Leaving home could also expose her to further danger without safe accommodation and practical support.

All the Ayatollah's men — ensuring the regime's survival

The concerns also extend to the online space. An investigation published by Human Rights Activists in Iran in October reported that the government-licensed matchmaking platform Adam and Eve displayed girls aged 13 to 17 as prospective spouses. Those findings do not establish how many marriages resulted, or whether the war increased them.

What can be done to protect girls?

Raeesi called for a minimum marriage age of 18 for both sexes, alongside preventive intervention, financial assistance, education and safe accommodation.

"Education alone is not enough," he said. Families also need the means to support their children.

Thompson urged targeted financial assistance, measures to keep girls in school, confidential reporting channels and independent legal support. Safe accommodation must be accessible without permission from guardians who may themselves be responsible for coercion, she said.

According to rights advocates, effective protection means that a girl under pressure to marry can say no without losing her home, her safety or her chance to continue school.

items.title: French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
items.summary: The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
items.body:
Europe

French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault

November 27, 20266:49 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

FILE - Actor Gerard Depardieu arrives to face trial for the alleged sexual assaults of two women on a film set in 2021, on March 24, 2025 in Paris.

Aurelien Morissard/AP

hide caption

Aurelien Morissard/AP

PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.

Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.

Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.

Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday's ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases.

The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.

The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.

A French cinema icon faces a #MeToo reckoning

With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.

He became one of the country's most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."

But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

On Nov. 16, Depardieu abandoned his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology that marked a departure from his earlier denials in that case.

"I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered," he said in a written statement.

Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters").

The court also ordered his name to be listed in France's national sex offender database.

"On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu said.

Accusations against Depardieu sparked a national debate

The controversy surrounding Depardieu intensified in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.

Even French President Emmanuel Macron weighed in, drawing criticism from women's rights activists when he said the actor "makes France proud." Macron invoked the presumption of innocence and said he would not participate in a "manhunt."

The controversy exposed divisions in a country where some prominent cultural figures had pushed back against the #MeToo movement.

In 2018, actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women signed an open letter defending men's freedom to make advances toward women and warning against what they saw as the movement's excesses.

Born in 1948 into a working-class family in the central French city of Châteauroux, Depardieu overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors. His career spanned hundreds of films, from "The Last Metro" and "Jean de Florette" to the popular "Asterix" franchise.

His excesses off-screen also made international headlines, notably when he accepted a Russian passport from Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

法国影星热拉尔·德帕迪约因强奸和性侵指控被勒令受审

2026年11月27日 上午6:49（美国东部时间）

作者

美联社

资料图——2025年3月24日，演员热拉尔·德帕迪约抵达巴黎，就2021年片场两名女性遭性侵的指控出庭受审。

奥雷利安·莫里萨尔/美联社

隐藏图注

奥雷利安·莫里萨尔/美联社

巴黎——当局周四表示，数十年来法国最负盛名的演员之一热拉尔·德帕迪约已被勒令就强奸和性侵一名年轻女演员的指控接受审判。此时距这位影星在另一起案件中放弃对性侵定罪判决的上诉不到两周。

女演员夏洛特·阿尔努尔2018年指控德帕迪约在其巴黎家中强奸她，当时她22岁。

八年后，巴黎上诉法院裁定，这位演员应就2018年8月7日强奸和性侵的指控接受审判，同时驳回了与六天后第二起事件相关的指控。

现年77岁的德帕迪约否认了强奸指控。他的律师德尔菲娜·梅耶告诉美联社，他对周四的裁决提出异议，但未说明是否会向法国最高民事和刑事法院提出挑战。

该裁决维持了调查法官2025年8月将德帕迪约送交审判的裁定的一部分。

此案已成为法国反思性暴力问题中最受关注的案件之一，因为#MeToo运动在该国遭遇阻力，尤其是在艺术界。

一位法国电影偶像面临#MeToo的清算

德帕迪约身材魁梧、鼻梁歪斜、银幕气场强大，统治法国影坛半个世纪。

他成为法国最知名的文化输出之一，凭《大鼻子情圣》获奥斯卡提名，凭《绿卡》获金球奖。

但性行为不当的指控及其随后的定罪，日益盖过他的电影成就。

11月16日，德帕迪约放弃对2021年片场性侵两名女性定罪判决的上诉，接受18个月缓刑，并公开道歉，这与他此前在该案中的否认态度截然不同。

“因此，我向那些可能受到伤害的人致以深切而真诚的歉意，”他在一份书面声明中说。

德帕迪约于2025年5月被判在拍摄《绿色百叶窗》期间猥亵一名布景师和一名助理罪名成立。

法院还下令将其姓名列入法国全国性犯罪者数据库。

“在片场，我长期以来一直躲在挑衅和粗俗幽默背后。我以为我的言语和一些行为没有后果。但事实并非如此，尤其是出自一个曾拥有我那样权力的人，”德帕迪约说。

对德帕迪约的指控引发全国辩论

2023年12月，一部电视纪录片显示他在2018年朝鲜之行期间多次发表淫秽言论并做出淫秽手势，围绕德帕迪约的争议随之加剧。

就连法国总统埃马纽埃尔·马克龙也介入其中，称这位演员“让法国骄傲”，招致女权活动人士的批评。马克龙援引无罪推定原则，并表示他不会参与“猎巫”。

这场争议暴露了该国的分歧，一些知名文化人物曾抵制#MeToo运动。

2018年，女演员凯瑟琳·德纳芙和其他99名女性签署公开信，捍卫男性向女性示好的自由，并警告她们所认为的运动过激行为。

德帕迪约1948年出生于法国中部城市沙托鲁的一个工人阶级家庭，克服语言障碍，成为法国最多产的演员之一。他的职业生涯横跨数百部电影，从《最后一班地铁》和《恋恋山城》到广受欢迎的《阿斯泰利克斯》系列。

他在银幕外的放纵行为也登上国际头条，尤其是2013年因法国税收纠纷接受俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京颁发的俄罗斯护照。

items.title: Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps but face hurdles and risks
items.summary: The number of Indians working in Germany has grown rapidly in recent years. But many continue to face challenges in the labor market. Some also fall victim to recruitment scams, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5Pyc6

Prefer DW on Google

Germany, facing a shrinking and rapidly aging population, is seeking skilled professionals in a number of sectors Image: Gunter Hübner/dpa/picture-alliance

Advertisement

Pratyay Saikia was studying food technology in 2022 when he saw an advertisement from Magic Billion, a recruitment agency that places skilled and semi-skilled Indian professionals in verified jobs abroad.

The 25-year-old from the northern Indian state of Haryana reached out to explore employment opportunities.

Four years later, he is working as a butcher at Metzgerei Lederer in southern Germany, having completed a three-year apprenticeship at the butcher shop.

"I came to Baden-Württemberg with 180 other Indians who came here to do an Ausbildung [apprenticeship] program. Me and seven others did our Ausbildung at Lederer [butcher shop], while others went into the construction sector. I now have a full-time job here," Saikia told DW.

He is not alone as the number of Indian workers subject to social security contributions in Germany has grown sevenfold over the past decade, to over 140,000 professionals.

Many of them work in the IT and health care sectors.

India meets German engineering

Pressing need for workers, but hesitant to hire

Germany, facing a shrinking and rapidly aging population, doesn't just need software specialists and nurses. It is also seeking skilled professionals such as electricians, mechatronics technicians, solar panel installers and truck drivers.

A 2024 study by Bertelsmann Foundation concluded that Germany needs 288,000 foreign skilled workers per year until 2040 to fill the shortage left by retiring workers. Another report from the consulting firm FMC Group noted that over 369,000 skilled job positions went unfilled in 2025.

Despite the pressing need for skilled workers, many firms, particularly Germany's renowned Mittelstand (small and medium-sized enterprises), are reluctant to recruit from places like India, say observers.

"Hiring an electrician from India is a relatively new concept for German companies, so they are hesitant," said Daniel Raja, managing director of NM NextMittelstand GmbH, a Düsseldorf-based recruitment firm focused on connecting German firms with skilled workers from India.

The Mittelstand companies are often overlooked by young talent abroad, while many of these firms are not actively recruiting international skilled workers, Raja said.

This disconnect, coupled with the often high German language requirements, means that many skilled positions remain unfilled, he explained.

Germany looks to India to address skilled labor shortage

Language a key hurdle

Kipp, the SWP expert, argued that preventing exploitative hiring practices requires streamlining migration procedures, expanding pre-departure cultural training and becoming more effective at identifying trusted entities and combating social media scams.

Hackers breach US Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform

Cloud One is among the US military's biggest cloud platforms.

FILE PHOTO: The Pentagon is seen from the air in Washington, U.S., March 3, 2022. REUTERS/Joshua Roberts/File Photo
